### 2026-10-20 – ## W3: Programmable Guitar Pedal

**5h**

## W3: Programmable Guitar Pedal
### Entry 1: Firmware tools & breadboard amplifiers

I have two options for creating my guitar pedal:

1. Buy a bunch of ICs and wire them together, costing me a lot and making the development of my PCB easy
2. Use passive components (eg. resistors, transistors, and capacitors) to do all the heavy lifting, including amplification and attenuation of the audio signals.

This session was spent exploring option two: this definitely felt like my preference at first, it seemed simpler and would allow me to learn more. This assumption turned out to be a mistake!!!

### Building a wireless voltmeter

I wanted to explore what voltages / currents I would be working with. I did have a voltmeter I could use, but I felt like I needed something a bit more visual - so I set out to create a voltmeter web application that I could run on my Raspberry Pi Pico, and access from my computer.

The code is a python web server:

![Screenshot 2026-10-20 at 15.39.48](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/3Z57nO3DOx0C7tgaKyZzjKBiZIWIGXGt/687c778fc99ef91bdf8f724cffebeacbdcbbf1f36bf5be089a1c6ff470c70662.png)

...that hosts a HTML canvas webpage:

![Screenshot 2026-10-20 at 15.40.14](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/3Z57nO3DOx0C7tgaKyZzjKBiZIWIGXGt/4af379d58f2e6a6b0e7d80002852a885d77aa027dd0b8b58932fd6880c31c1be.png)

...which looks like the following (in this example I connected my computer's audio jack output to the voltmeter):

![IMG_8415 Large](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/3Z57nO3DOx0C7tgaKyZzjKBiZIWIGXGt/aa1748652dc69f503e1c53f5a452141446467759f73f7414ead43baf3ed1241f.jpg)

### Building (attemping to build) the signal amplifiers

This is where my efforts to fulfil option 2 fell a bit apart...

I started by creating a single-transistor voltage amplifier with a breadboard, some resistors, and some capacitors:

![IMG_8419 Large](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/3Z57nO3DOx0C7tgaKyZzjKBiZIWIGXGt/2ec1f364c5d9075660464adeb26821e6482d00cdb983a6ce0d5aaffad637f99a.jpg)

While this appeared to help amplify the audio jack output, it only worked when I set my laptop to a high volume. This wasn't good news, as even the quietest line-level (consumer audio) signal is about ~100 times larger than my acoustic guitar output.

And so I had to switch strategies, creating a two:

![IMG_8422 Large](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/3Z57nO3DOx0C7tgaKyZzjKBiZIWIGXGt/626b0ccf3fde1bd99830f67099d9cff2490f47eea8f7f86901b85fc14b6c06f6.jpg)

...and then 3 transistor breadboard circuit:

![IMG_8423 Large](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/3Z57nO3DOx0C7tgaKyZzjKBiZIWIGXGt/945210a839715be53b08a017fa3c95c50c92148ab84dc3a34e2ede49e50848e3.jpg)

However, as the previous image shows, the extra amplification didn't seem to improve the amplitude of the output audio signal. It was at this point that I realised I kindddd of don't have much of a clue what I'm doing...

This session may have seemed like a waste of time, however it did rule option 2 off the table, which means I'll revert to a setup of buying dedicated audio ICs (eg. pre-amps, ADC / DACs) and simply connect them up in KiCad.

Next session will therefore be deciding which specific functionality, and therefore components, I want in my pedal.

Thanks for reading :)

### 2026-10-20 – ## W3: Programmable guitar pedal

**4h**

## W3: Programmable guitar pedal
### Finalising design, sourcing components

This session was spent finalising the layout and sourcing the components for the guitar pedal, experimenting with my guitar amplifier and creating the bill of materials in my GitHub repository.

I first created the following flow diagram showing the design of the pedal:

![IMG_8428 Large](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/3Z57nO3DOx0C7tgaKyZzjKBiZIWIGXGt/2f53057494e8554a0e52c99e22896e15b9cce3266c5d448f7d5ee521739d7d2d.jpg)

I definitely tried to use as few components as possible, looking to keep the costs down. One example is this test of line level audio with my guitar amplifier. I initially thought direct audio would be too hot for the amplifier, however this test showed that I wouldn't need any attenuation of the DAC output. These little savings help simplify my design, and make sure I don't go over budget.

![IMG_8427 Large](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/3Z57nO3DOx0C7tgaKyZzjKBiZIWIGXGt/1440a0b01d0a041354e0ecf4f7967d33004a0f2b1496a8d21b4df9756cf349a7.jpg)

The rest of the time was spent sourcing my components. I initially wanted to source all my components from LCSC, as I could ship this with my PCB and 3D-printing orders, saving money. However, this was found to be impractical, and I ended up sourcing components from 3 seperate places.

Some components were especially important to get, such as the Pico 2 WH, which was an in-built FPU perfect for fast digital signal processing, which was definitely needed here:

![Screenshot 2026-10-20 at 17.53.51](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/3Z57nO3DOx0C7tgaKyZzjKBiZIWIGXGt/6df598dc20475d8533b832b5c468911f5b5802efdc8ecada1a6b1dd541981911.png)

I ended up with the following:

```
JLC (shipping ~$5) - all in USD {

JLCPCB ~$10
JLC3DP ~$5

LCSC:
  * Guitar inputs (C41409495): 2 * $0.5 = $1    https://www.lcsc.com/product-detail/C41409495.html
  * Potentiometers (C470717): 3 * $0.57 = $1.71 https://www.lcsc.com/product-detail/C470717.html
  * Op-Amp (C5213) 5 * $0.22 = $1.11            https://www.lcsc.com/product-detail/C5213.html
}

Core Electronics (shipping ~$10) - all in AUD:
    * Raspberry Pi Pico WH $14.30 https://core-electronics.com.au/raspberry-pi-pico-2-wh-with-headers.html
    * Battery $5.55               https://core-electronics.com.au/polymer-lithium-ion-battery-400mah-38456.html
    * Charger $6.85               https://core-electronics.com.au/makerverse-usb-c-lipo-charger.html
    * DAC $8.05                   https://core-electronics.com.au/adafruit-pcm5100-i2s-dac-line-level-output-100db-snr.html
    * Headers (2 x $0.35 = $0.70) https://core-electronics.com.au/0-100-2-54-mm-female-header-1x20-pin-straight.html

Jaycar - all in AUD:
    * 6.5mm audio cable $12.25    https://www.jaycar.com.au/6-5mm-mono-plug-to-6-5mm-mono-r-a-plug-audio-cable-3m/p/WA7024

approx cost ~$64 USD = 13 hours of work
```

The BOM turned out like the following, and can now be found in the GitHub repo for this project:

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/3Z57nO3DOx0C7tgaKyZzjKBiZIWIGXGt/4c6216eedbd0b51a3572b7c421fa42a6df3277aea45e499c3cc0fad8cdbbc2e9.png)

Thanks for reading :)

## W3: Programmable Guitar Pedal

The others couldn't as readily be found online - these ones I had to design myself in KiCad (using experience I had from my W1 Rubber Ducky project).

The USB-C LiPo charger ended up like the following:

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/3Z57nO3DOx0C7tgaKyZzjKBiZIWIGXGt/f627178b0ae05866147e94634fe41977e6ad1afed5918f72c2383d98bbe073d4.png)

![IMG_8429 Large](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/3Z57nO3DOx0C7tgaKyZzjKBiZIWIGXGt/c83414f2913b146837d37d5d549a3d9058af91d44e70865ab1b6266a69e6bca5.jpg)

I then completed the DAC audio output circuit and audio attenuator:

![IMG_8433 Large](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/3Z57nO3DOx0C7tgaKyZzjKBiZIWIGXGt/267ea10e4a78a6d811f013b27705f04e376a362bf4ed8c19b495257ad725e3e3.jpg)

...and the op-amp circuit (which was wayyy more complicated than I thought it would be):

![Journal image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/3Z57nO3DOx0C7tgaKyZzjKBiZIWIGXGt/137e0a4c03ba5d1600d1e8002ba62a6d84ffaa67b0519ca526a0c0a7ca754198.jpg)

The final wiring ended up like the following:

![IMG_8435 Large](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/3Z57nO3DOx0C7tgaKyZzjKBiZIWIGXGt/f0b718931d2186d82c7d404f86ce4f844146ce0695a9a4b5924c7810f29709f0.jpg)

### 2026-10-21 – ## W3: Programmable Guitar Pedal

**4h**

## W3: Programmable Guitar Pedal
### Routing the PCB

This session was spent routing the PCB.

I first needed to finalise the components and footprints I would be using for my board. One change I made was using a precision 1M ohm pentiometer rather than one with a knob, as I originally had planned. Once a good gain setting for the guitar has been set, this setting would no longer need to be touched, so I found it straightforward to hide this setting from everyday use, giving me more control and precision.

![Screenshot 2026-10-21 at 19.56.49](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/3Z57nO3DOx0C7tgaKyZzjKBiZIWIGXGt/a5283986bfdc908019c8530505eab5861201a09fb0dbe20b9d848678abc629da.png)

I then placed the components approximately where I wanted them to end up, keeping all the inputs / outputs on the one side. Note the Pico's Micro USB would not need to be accessed during everyday use and therefore could be hidden away on the opposite side of the board:

![IMG_8441 Large](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/3Z57nO3DOx0C7tgaKyZzjKBiZIWIGXGt/7c22fbd666483ba1d5b7bbb2db733e6acab8806218100315405722dc1c561065.jpg)

![IMG_8444 Large](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/3Z57nO3DOx0C7tgaKyZzjKBiZIWIGXGt/4321dd6de1f11a9a22cbc101fa5fcf98a6bbd93fa0e7477292fe34af864d0f73.jpg)

I then routed my pins, and added a ground fill on the underside:

![IMG_8445 Large](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/3Z57nO3DOx0C7tgaKyZzjKBiZIWIGXGt/0ee3a0d2484199b1c6bdbf2265626ea3aaef8ca0138daf772fedfd0de623b021.jpg)

I ended up with the following:

![IMG_8447 Large](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/3Z57nO3DOx0C7tgaKyZzjKBiZIWIGXGt/4c4e9b318760f236d2191a16e187d5944da30cfbb99d95736dfaf02ea1a44d42.jpg)

I have to say I'm quite happy with the compact, 10cm by 5cm design, and I feel I've struck a good balance between audio quality, simplicity, and features in my PCB.

After passing ERC and DRC, I exported the Gerbers to my GitHub repository, ready for printing.

All thats left to do now is assemble the 3D-printed enclosure, and program the firmware of the Pico.

Thanks for reading!

### 2026-10-24 – ## W3: Programmable guitar pedal

**1.5h**

## W3: Programmable guitar pedal
### Firmware & FX

This session was spent designing the firmware for the pedal, specifically working out how to implement some basic guitar effect in code.

I started by working with overdrive, distortion, and fuzz: I used Desmos to work out good waveforms for each of these effects, which I then implemented in my Micropython code.

![Screenshot 2026-10-25 at 09.46.06](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/3Z57nO3DOx0C7tgaKyZzjKBiZIWIGXGt/a8872d77c9a7f9cfe54ba2c2078bc0b6dd14db5647d592f4fa927b5d4ac5e3c3.png)

![Screenshot 2026-10-25 at 09.40.28](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/3Z57nO3DOx0C7tgaKyZzjKBiZIWIGXGt/5275de8a5ef2e96e7f5136c738cc5d10c3f7e18049678cc3d93c8019c5666f4a.png)

I also created effects for reverb and echo.

![Screenshot 2026-10-25 at 09.40.17](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/3Z57nO3DOx0C7tgaKyZzjKBiZIWIGXGt/4be1a35a0fff302640284929cb94b104ac99f496b06692a2fe21f6f05a3e268d.png)

After doing some basic Python audio I/O, I used these basic functions to test a few effects using a recording of me playing the guitar.

The full code, as well as example guitar I/O can be found on my [GitHub](https://github.com/he1ias/programmable-guitar-pedal).

All that's left to do is the pedal's case (although I may have run out of time for it at this point, and it isn't strictly required).

Thanks for reading :)

### 2026-10-25 – ## W3: Programmable guitar pedal

**0.5h**

## W3: Programmable guitar pedal
### Finalising & submitting

This short session was spent finalising BOM.csv, my README.md and my GitHub repo, ready to submit.

Note that I ran out of time to implement the pedal casing. I also removed the battery functionality of the pedal, as I wanted to cut costs and I felt that this part of my project was unescessary, and complicated things.

As the charger only connects to the Pi's VSYS, nothing else about my design needed to change. I will keep the PCB the same so I can add this functionality back in in the future.
